title: How to Discover Small Tools That Solve Specific Problems
content:
A tiny utility can save an hour every week, or quietly add another account, data exposure, and maintenance obligation. Discovering useful small tools starts with a specific friction point, not a catalogue of popular apps. Describe the job in one sentence: “I need to compare two JSON responses without uploading customer data.” That sentence gives you a way to search, evaluate, and decline candidates.

Define the smallest job

Record the input, output, frequency, and consequence of an error. Is the input public text, internal source code, or customer data? Must the tool run offline? Does it need to integrate with an existing workflow? Is the result disposable, or will colleagues rely on it? These constraints matter more than the length of a feature list. A tool that handles five adjacent tasks may be less useful than a simple utility that handles one safely.

Try the built-in option first: editor command, browser feature, operating-system utility, or a short reproducible script. If it fits, you may avoid another vendor relationship. If it does not, record the exact missing capability before searching. Search terms should name the operation and data type, such as “local JSON diff utility,” rather than broad phrases such as “best productivity tools.” Treat ranking pages as discovery leads, not validation.

Inspect provenance and permissions

Find the maintainer's official site or repository, installation path, support channel, and recent release notes. GitHub documents that releases package software and are based on tags; a release page can help you identify what version you are evaluating. A recent release is a maintenance signal, not proof of security or suitability. Check whether the project's documentation explains supported platforms and how updates are delivered.

For an open-source candidate, inspect the actual license and redistribution terms. The Open Source Initiative's definition makes clear that source availability alone does not establish open-source rights. “Code visible on a repository” is insufficient if the license is absent or incompatible with your intended use. For a hosted service, read the provider's data-handling and retention terms directly; do not infer them from an “AI-powered” or “privacy-first” label.

List every permission requested by an extension or desktop app and connect it to the job. A color picker may need access to the active page, but a broad request to read all sites deserves closer scrutiny. Check whether the tool sends content to a remote server, can work locally, or requires an account. Do not test it with sensitive material until those answers are clear. If the documentation is silent, treat the uncertainty as a factor in the decision.

Run a bounded trial

Use a representative but non-sensitive sample. Measure setup time, number of steps, output correctness, and cleanup burden. Run the same task in each candidate. For a JSON comparison utility, include reordered keys, an array change, a missing property, and malformed input. A pretty interface is not enough if the result hides a meaningful difference or fails silently on invalid data.

Observe the output format. Can it be copied into the existing work item? Is there an export path that preserves context? Does the tool force a new destination where results disappear from team records? A personal convenience becomes a team dependency only when another person can understand the input, repeat the operation, and access the result appropriately.

Estimate total cost as more than subscription price. Include onboarding, permission review, migration of saved work, future updates, and the cost of an incorrect result. A free utility can be expensive if each teammate spends time reconciling its output. Conversely, a paid tool might justify its cost for a frequent, bounded task. Use your own observed workload and explicit assumptions rather than a generic return-on-investment claim.

Hypothetical example: choosing a local JSON comparator

Imagine a hypothetical small team comparing configuration exports every Friday. Their constraint is that the files include internal hostnames, so they need a local workflow. Candidate A is a hosted diff page with a polished interface but unclear upload retention. Candidate B is a local editor extension with narrow file access and a documented release history. Candidate C is an existing command-line diff that marks line changes but makes structural JSON differences hard to read.

The team creates synthetic exports with one changed value, reordered keys, and a removed array item. They time a single pass, inspect whether each difference is visible, and note the permissions required. They may choose the editor extension for a trial, keep the command-line option as a fallback, and reject the hosted page for this data class until its handling is clear. This is an editorial decision exercise, not a measured product comparison.

Checklist before keeping a small tool

  • Name the one job and the data classification.
  • Check whether an existing tool already covers it.
  • Use the official installation source and identify the evaluated version.
  • Read the license, permissions, update path, and data terms.
  • Compare candidates on the same safe sample and failure cases.
  • Record where results live and how a teammate could repeat them.
  • Set a review date or remove the tool if the use case disappears.

A good small tool earns a small, clear place in a workflow. Keep a short note explaining why it was chosen, what data it may handle, and what would trigger a replacement. That record helps the next teammate discover the tool without inheriting an unexplained collection of apps.
excerpt: Find small tools by defining one recurring job, checking provenance and permissions, and comparing candidates with a safe, repeatable trial.
